output:
*Interview with Mademoiselle Lina Ruedi, régleuse, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Mademoiselle Ruedi, I know this has been a dreadful thing to come to. Sit wherever you are comfortable. I only want to hear about the evening, in your own way and in your own order.

MLLE RUEDI: I cannot take it in, Monsieur. I keep expecting him to come down the stairs and tell me my pivots are out of true. He would have, too. He always found something.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the dinner.

MLLE RUEDI: When the temple struck nine, the master made us all take out our watches and show them to him, as he does every year. He told each owner what was wrong with theirs. Mine was exact, and he said so, which he did not say often. The doctor's was two minutes ahead. Monsieur Girard would not take his out of his pocket at all.

MATTHEY: Thank you. And after dinner?

MLLE RUEDI: I worked beside the master in the atelier, as I always did. The hall clock downstairs struck ten when the regulator showed twelve minutes to ten. He said what he always says about that clock. It is an old joke in the house, and I would rather not repeat it now. When the temple struck ten, the regulator agreed with the bell exactly.

MATTHEY: You are sure of that?

MLLE RUEDI: I am sure of the regulator, Monsieur. I set its beat myself, most of it. I know what it does.

MATTHEY: When did he send you downstairs?

MLLE RUEDI: When the regulator showed twenty past ten. He sent me down, and I went straight down to the kitchen. The regulator was running then, and he was well. I want you to write that down exactly. He was well.

MATTHEY: Yes. Did you see him at any other time that day?

MLLE RUEDI: That afternoon I saw him in the kitchen with Rosa's clock in his hands. He was laughing. I did not ask him why. One does not ask the master why.

MATTHEY: And in the kitchen, after you went down?

MLLE RUEDI: I stayed in the kitchen with Rosa. When Madame's piano began, I looked at the kitchen clock, which is Rosa's American alarm clock, and it showed two minutes to eleven. When the piano stopped, the kitchen clock showed eleven minutes past eleven. I stayed in the kitchen with Rosa until after the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: You have worked on his repeater with him, I think.

MLLE RUEDI: Four years, Monsieur. Four years of his hands and mine on one movement. He meant it to speak at the turn of the century.

MATTHEY: Could you explain to me how it speaks? I confess I do not know.

MLLE RUEDI: When you press the slide, it gives the hours in low notes. Each quarter is a doubled note. Then the minutes past the quarter come in high notes, one for each minute. It is not a difficult thing to hear once you know the pattern, but it takes a great deal of work to make it true. He would not let a single note be a hair out.

MATTHEY: And your own watch?

MLLE RUEDI: I regulated it myself. I have never trusted anyone else with it, and I do not intend to start now.

MATTHEY: Do you have any idea who might have wished him harm?

MLLE RUEDI: I do not speculate, Monsieur. I know what I saw and what I heard, and I have told you. The rest is for you to find out, not for me to guess at.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you have not told me that you think I should know?

MLLE RUEDI: Only that he was the best master I ever worked for, and that he was exact about everything, even about people. He would not have wanted this written down badly. Please write it correctly.
